clue.text: Get overhead protection by embracing revolution

indicators.note: to embrace is to hold in the arms, so the first piece wraps round the second

parts.note: a roll is one turn or revolution

explanation.surface: Someone seeks cover from above by taking up a revolutionary cause.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Get' is a link word; 'by' is used as its own letters, opened up to hold ROLL.
explanation.definitionFit: An umbrella, colloquially a brolly, shields the head from rain falling from above.

clue.text: Rescue from bilge?

definitions.meaning: a financial rescue of a failing firm
scooping water out of a boat's bilge with a bucket

explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means both a rescue package and the act of emptying water from a boat.

clue.text: Source of colour from Loch Resort

indicators.note: from means the letters are taken out of the following words

explanation.surface: A Scottish lochside resort supplies a pigment.
explanation.definitionFit: This earthy yellow-brown pigment is a classic source of colour for painters.

clue.text: Land of the French emperor

parts.note: les is French for the (plural)
Otho was a Roman emperor in AD 69

explanation.surface: A country belonging to the French emperor.
explanation.definitionFit: This African kingdom is a land, a country enclosed by South Africa.

clue.text: Reptile takes American bulb

parts.note: croc is short for crocodile, a reptile
US is short for United States, hence American

explanation.surface: A reptile makes off with an American light bulb.
explanation.definitionFit: The plant grows from a corm, which gardeners loosely call a bulb, so it stands as an example.

clue.text: Draws Sir 12 for the amateur …

definitions.meaning: the gentleman thief created by E W Hornung, the amateur cracksman

explanation.walkthrough: 12 is STAMFORD, so Sir 12 is Sir Stamford, founder of Singapore. The ellipsis leads on to 6: Hornung's A J Raffles was The Amateur Cracksman.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means prize draws, Sir Stamford the colonial founder, and Hornung's gentleman burglar.

clue.text: … joker that breaks in?

parts.note: a joker cracks jokes, so he is a man who cracks; one who cracks safes is a burglar

explanation.walkthrough: Continuing from 5, the gentleman burglar Raffles was the amateur version of this.
explanation.definitionFit: The old word is a burglar or safebreaker, one who cracks safes and breaks into houses.

clue.text: Nader the stabiliser — so peril's averted

indicators.note: averted means turned aside, so the letters are turned into a new order

parts.note: the 's only shows possession or stands for 'is', so it adds no letters: the word before it gives these letters as it is written

explanation.surface: Ralph Nader is called a stabiliser, so danger is avoided.
explanation.walkthrough: Ralph Nader was called the spoiler of the 2000 US election; a car's rear aerofoil is also a stabilising spoiler.
explanation.definitionFit: A candidate who takes votes from a front-runner is a spoiler, and so is the aerofoil that steadies a fast car.

clue.text: Ought to be quiet when dreadfully loud

parts.note: sh is a call for quiet

indicators.note: dreadfully suggests the word is badly mangled

explanation.surface: Someone should keep quiet when it gets terribly noisy.
explanation.definitionFit: Both express obligation: you ought to go means you have a duty to go.

clue.text: Lofty American style has entered eighth work with bottle (British), stealing round with housefly just half swallowed …

indicators.note: to enter is to go inside, so the word has goes into the rearranged letters
to work something is to knead or rework it, so the letters of eighth are rearranged

parts.note: a flagon is a large bottle

indicators.note: the word for stealing goes round the British piece, enclosing it

parts.note: theft is the act of stealing
our, from the British setter's point of view, means British
HO is the abbreviation for house, the first part of housefly

indicators.note: something swallowed is taken inside, so the half-word goes into fly

parts.note: the second part of housefly is fly

indicators.note: just half of the word just, its first two letters

explanation.surface: A rambling description of an American bottle-stealer with a half-swallowed fly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'work' rearranges eighth to HIGTHE before 'entered' opens it. 'just half' takes JU. The phrase is from the South Pacific song A Wonderful Guy; 'Lofty American style' defines it.
explanation.definitionFit: The song simile describes elation as being up as high as a flag hoisted on America's Independence Day, a lofty height in a distinctly American idiom.

clue.text: … two little houses a little earlier, I assure you!

parts.note: HO is the short form of house
a nest is a small home, a little house for birds

indicators.note: only a little of the phrase is used, so its last letter is cut off

parts.note: following on from the Fourth of July in the previous clue, earlier means in June

explanation.surface: A speaker swears to the truth while mentioning two small houses and an earlier date.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis ties this to the Fourth of July at 24: a little earlier than that is IN JUNE, docked of its E by 'a little'.
explanation.definitionFit: The dated American idiom is an emphatic assurance of truthfulness, a way of swearing that one is being straight.

clue.text: Odds against posh cathedral town being on the back burner

parts.note: U means upper class, hence posh

indicators.note: putting the word on its back turns it round, so it is read backwards

parts.note: a kiln is a furnace for burning or firing pottery
Ely is a cathedral city in Cambridgeshire

explanation.surface: A posh cathedral town has its plans shelved, which seems improbable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on the back burner' looks like one idiom, but 'burner' is KILN and 'on the back' reverses it to NLIK.
explanation.definitionFit: When the odds are against something, it is improbable, so the phrase works as an adjective for an outcome not expected.

clue.text: Harold's success at Chelsea the way to early crossings

definitions.meaning: King Harold beat the Norwegian invaders at this battle in 1066
the London football club Chelsea play at this ground
the phrase reads as a ford leading on to a ..., early ways over rivers

explanation.walkthrough: Harold II won here weeks before losing at Hastings; Chelsea's home ground has the same name.
explanation.definitionFit: The Yorkshire battlefield of Harold's victory and Chelsea's stadium share this name, which literally combines a ford and a bridge.

clue.text: Imperious males involved with turf

indicators.note: involved means tangled together, so the letters are mixed

explanation.surface: Domineering men are mixed up in horse racing.
explanation.definitionFit: Both describe someone who commands others with a powerful, domineering manner.

clue.text: A few keep partly bright, or not at all

indicators.note: to keep something is to hold it inside, so the word for a few goes round the pick

parts.note: some means a few

indicators.note: only part of bright is taken, its first two letters

explanation.surface: Some people retain a little brightness, or perhaps none at all.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition leans on the preceding 'bright': 'not at all' bright means dark and gloomy.
explanation.definitionFit: Something gloomy and dark is not bright in the least, which is what the clue's closing phrase suggests.

clue.text: Singular science for Macbeth's dogs?

definitions.meaning: the science of matter and energy, ..., reduced to a singular form
Macbeth says throw medicine to the dogs, wanting none of it

explanation.walkthrough: In Macbeth Act 5 the king says 'Throw physic to the dogs; I'll none of it', meaning medicine.
explanation.definitionFit: The archaic word for medicine looks like a singular of physics, and Macbeth tells the doctor to throw it to the dogs.

clue.text: Stag holding out had requirement for building site

indicators.note: holding means containing, so the deer's word wraps round the rest

parts.note: a hart is a male deer, a stag

indicators.note: out suggests the letters are put out of order

explanation.surface: A stag holds out, needing something for a construction site.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stag' looks like a party, but it is the deer; 'out' rearranges 'had' to DHA, and a hard hat is safety headgear.
explanation.definitionFit: Protective helmets are compulsory on building sites, so one is a requirement there.

clue.text: Finish with remedy for the Spanish invasion

indicators.note: an invasion goes into a territory, so the Spanish word goes inside

parts.note: a cure is a remedy
los is Spanish for the (plural)

explanation.surface: A cure for a Spanish invasion ends things.
explanation.definitionFit: Both nouns mean the ending or conclusion of something, as when a business reaches its end.

clue.text: Car number of setter, usually less than the day of 24

definitions.text: usually less than the day of 24

parts.note: auto is short for automobile, a car
the setter speaking of himself would say my

explanation.surface: The setter's car registration is usually lower than a date.
explanation.walkthrough: The day of 24 (the Fourth of July) is Independence Day; self-rule short of full independence is usually less than that.
explanation.definitionFit: Self-government within a larger state usually falls short of full independence, the thing America celebrates on that day.

clue.text: A little insect's English relative

parts.note: a gnat is a small fly

explanation.surface: A tiny English insect turns out to be a relation.
explanation.definitionFit: This term names a kinsman descended through the male line, a type of relative.

clue.text: Bad lot, I fancy, in the paper

indicators.note: fancy as a verb means imagine, and as an adjective elaborate, either way rearranging

explanation.surface: Someone imagines a rogue appears in the newspaper.
explanation.definitionFit: A popular small-format newspaper is a paper, often a sensationalist one.

clue.text: Non-wizards reported horse among hybrids

indicators.note: among puts the horse inside the word for hybrids

parts.note: mules are hybrids of horse and donkey
gee-gee, a child's word for horse, said as two letters gives GG

explanation.surface: Ordinary people say a horse has been seen among hybrid animals.
explanation.walkthrough: Gee-gee is British nursery talk for a horse; spoken, it is the letter G twice.
explanation.definitionFit: In the Harry Potter books people without magic are called by this word, so non-wizards fits.

clue.text: Making for Berne like Americans after 24?

indicators.note: making something is constructing it, so the letters are put together anew

explanation.surface: Someone heading for the Swiss capital is compared to Americans after independence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Making for' looks like heading towards, but 'Making' is the anagram signal working on 'for Berne'.
explanation.definitionFit: After the Fourth of July 1776 Americans were born free citizens rather than colonial subjects.

clue.text: See 12
See 10
See 9
Agricultural worker at back of boat?

definitions.meaning: one who tills, working the soil
the steering handle fixed at the stern of a boat

explanation.definitionFit: The word means both a farmer who tills land and the lever at the stern used to steer.

clue.text: Fuss about wrongdoing with good looker

parts.note: ado means fuss

indicators.note: about means turned round, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: sin is wrongdoing

explanation.surface: Fussing over misbehaviour with a handsome partner.
explanation.definitionFit: The handsome youth of Greek myth gives his name to any very attractive man.
